--- title: "Week 03: Data and Exploration" --- ## [03a] Strings / Factors / Packages ### Topics - Strings - Factors - Packages ### Readings - [View on Canvas](https://canvas.ku.edu/courses/{{< meta canvas-id >}}/files/folder/Unit%20A){target="_blank"} ### Slides ```{=html} ``` ::: {.fsmaller} \*Note that you can click the three-line (hamburger) icon on the bottom-left of the slides to access a navigation menu. You can click inside the slides region and press the left and right arrow keys on your keyboard to advance and reverse the slides and animations. ::: ### Practice #### Question 1 a) Create a character vector named `flavors` that contains the following strings and print it to the console: - Cookies & Cream - Americone Dream (R) - Bob Marley's 1 Love b) Use a function to calculate the number of strings in `flavors`. c) Use another function to calculate the number of characters in each string in `flavors`. d) Let R know how you feel about ice cream by using a function to either make all the characters in `flavors` uppercase (you LOVE ice cream) or lowercase (you don't love ice cream). {{< dstart summary="Answer key" >}} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Part (a) flavors <- c("Cookies & Cream", "Americone Dream (R)", "Bob Marley's 1 Love") flavors ## [1] "Cookies & Cream" "Americone Dream (R)" "Bob Marley's 1 Love" # Part (b) length(flavors) ## [1] 3 # Part (c) nchar(flavors) ## [1] 15 19 19 # Part (d) toupper(flavors) ## [1] "COOKIES & CREAM" "AMERICONE DREAM (R)" "BOB MARLEY'S 1 LOVE" tolower(flavors) ## [1] "cookies & cream" "americone dream (r)" "bob marley's 1 love" ``` ::: {{< dstop >}} #### Question 2 Ebi has tracked her spending over two weeks. Every time she makes a purchase on items that are not food, she writes down a code representing the day of the week (e.g., 1 = Sunday and 2 = Monday). At the end of the week, she has the following codes written down: 1 2 2 4 7 1 1 5 6 7. a) Create a numerical vector (not a factor) called `ebi_num` that contains these codes. Print it to the console. b) Turn `ebi_num` into a factor object called `ebi_fct` with levels 1, 2, ..., 7 and labels "Sun", "Mon", ..., "Sat". Print it to the console. c) Use the `table()` function on `ebi_num` and then on `ebi_fct`. Compare their output. Which version do you prefer and why? {{< dstart summary="Answer key" >}} **Answer (a)** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ebi_num <- c(1, 2, 2, 4, 7, 1, 1, 5, 6, 7) ebi_num ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 2 2 4 7 1 1 5 6 7 ``` ::: ::: **Answer (b)** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ebi_fct <- factor( ebi_num, levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7), labels = c("Sun", "Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat") ) ebi_fct ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] Sun Mon Mon Wed Sat Sun Sun Thu Fri Sat Levels: Sun Mon Tue Wed Thu Fri Sat ``` ::: ::: **Answer (c)** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} table(ebi_num) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ebi_num 1 2 4 5 6 7 3 2 1 1 1 2 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} table(ebi_fct) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ebi_fct Sun Mon Tue Wed Thu Fri Sat 3 2 0 1 1 1 2 ``` ::: ::: I prefer the factor version because it includes the labels at the top, which is convenient, and it also includes the zero count for "Tue", whereas the numerical version omits it. This makes it easier to see that Tuesdays had the fewest purchases for Ebi. {{< dstop >}} #### Question 3 a) Install the `tidyverse` package. It may take several minutes to install because it contains several sub-packages that we will use in this class. b) Check if the `tidyverse` package has a website and/or vignettes. Read the "Welcome to the tidyverse" vignette (it is relatively brief and will prepare you for next week). {{< dstart summary="Answer key" >}} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Part (a) install.packages("tidyverse") # or RStudio > Extras pane > Packages tab > Install button # Part (b) browseVignettes("tidyverse") # or RStudio > Extras Pane > Packages tab > search for tidyverse > click globe icon > check website for Articles ``` ::: {{< dstop >}} --- *Note that there is no need to turn in Activities. These are just for practice!* ## [03b] Data Frames / Files / Exploration ### Topics - Data Frames - Data Files - Data Exploration ### Files - [salaries.csv](../../data/salaries.csv){download="salaries.csv"} - [salaries0.csv](../../data/salaries0.csv){download="salaries0.csv"} - [gradebook.csv](../../data/gradebook.csv){download="gradebook.csv"} ### Readings - [View on Canvas](https://canvas.ku.edu/courses/{{< meta canvas-id >}}/files/folder/Unit%20A){target="_blank"} ### Slides ```{=html} ``` ::: {.fsmaller} \*Note that you can click the three-line (hamburger) icon on the bottom-left of the slides to access a navigation menu. You can click inside the slides region and press the left and right arrow keys on your keyboard to advance and reverse the slides and animations. ::: ### Practice #### Question 1 The following table summarizes the season information for the eight seasons of AMC's *Breaking Bad* show. a) Tidy up this data and save it to a tibble. Decide for yourself how to handle season 5 (should it be a single observation or two?). For the first and last aired dates, just store the year as a number. b) Save the tibble you created to a CSV file named "breaking_bad.csv". ![](../../img/breaking_bad_wikipedia.png) {{< dstart summary="Answer key" >}} **Part (a)** Version with one observation for the season five parts ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) season <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5) episodes <- c(7, 13, 13, 13, 16) first_air <- c(2008, 2009, 2010, 2011, 2012) last_air <- c(2008, 2009, 2010, 2011, 2013) network <- "AMC" breaking_bad <- tibble(season, episodes, first_air, last_air, network) breaking_bad ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 5 season episodes first_air last_air network 1 1 7 2008 2008 AMC 2 2 13 2009 2009 AMC 3 3 13 2010 2010 AMC 4 4 13 2011 2011 AMC 5 5 16 2012 2013 AMC ``` ::: ::: Version with two separate observations for the season five parts ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) season <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5.1, 5.2) episodes <- c(7, 13, 13, 13, 8, 8) first_air <- c(2008, 2009, 2010, 2011, 2012, 2013) last_air <- c(2008, 2009, 2010, 2011, 2012, 2013) network <- "AMC" breaking_bad <- tibble(season, episodes, first_air, last_air, network) breaking_bad ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 × 5 season episodes first_air last_air network 1 1 7 2008 2008 AMC 2 2 13 2009 2009 AMC 3 3 13 2010 2010 AMC 4 4 13 2011 2011 AMC 5 5.1 8 2012 2012 AMC 6 5.2 8 2013 2013 AMC ``` ::: ::: **Part (b)** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} write_csv(breaking_bad, "breaking_bad.csv") ``` ::: {{< dstop >}} #### Question 2 a) Download the `kaggle_cereal.csv` file from Canvas and save it to your class Project folder. b) Use \{tidyverse\} to import this file into R as a tibble named `cereal`, using an argument to make the missing values (coded as `"missing"`) into `NA`s. c) Run your command again but with the `show_col_types = FALSE` argument to suppress the column specification message. {{< dstart summary="Answer key" >}} **Part (b)** ::: {.cell replace_path='["../../data/",""]'} ```{.r .cell-code} cereal <- read_csv("../../data/kaggle_cereal.csv", na = "missing") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Rows: 77 Columns: 8 ── Column specification ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Delimiter: "," chr (3): name, mfr, type dbl (5): calories, sodium, carbo, sugars, rating ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data. ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message. ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cereal ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 77 × 8 name mfr type calories sodium carbo sugars rating 1 100% Bran Nabisco cold 70 130 5 6 68.4 2 100% Natural Bran Quaker O… cold 120 15 8 8 34.0 3 All-Bran Kelloggs cold 70 260 7 5 59.4 4 All-Bran with Extra Fiber Kelloggs cold 50 140 8 0 93.7 5 Almond Delight Ralston … cold 110 200 14 8 34.4 6 Apple Cinnamon Cheerios General … cold 110 180 10.5 10 29.5 7 Apple Jacks Kelloggs cold 110 125 11 14 33.2 8 Basic 4 General … cold 130 210 18 8 37.0 9 Bran Chex Ralston … cold 90 200 15 6 49.1 10 Bran Flakes Post cold 90 210 13 5 53.3 # ℹ 67 more rows ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cereal <- read_csv("../../data/kaggle_cereal.csv", na = "missing", show_col_types = FALSE) ``` ::: {{< dstop >}} #### Question 3 a) Update the `cereal` tibble from Question 2 to make the `type` variable a factor. b) Tabulate the `type` variable using `data_tabulate()` and plot its discrete distribution using `qplot()`. c) Describe the `calories` variable using `describe_distribution()` and plot its continuous distribution using `qplot()` and a "histogram" or "boxplot" geom. d) Plot the covariation of the `calories` and `rating` variables using `qplot()` and a "point" or "jitter" geom. {{< dstart summary="Answer key" >}} **Part (a)** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cereal$type <- factor(cereal$type) cereal ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 77 × 8 name mfr type calories sodium carbo sugars rating 1 100% Bran Nabisco cold 70 130 5 6 68.4 2 100% Natural Bran Quaker O… cold 120 15 8 8 34.0 3 All-Bran Kelloggs cold 70 260 7 5 59.4 4 All-Bran with Extra Fiber Kelloggs cold 50 140 8 0 93.7 5 Almond Delight Ralston … cold 110 200 14 8 34.4 6 Apple Cinnamon Cheerios General … cold 110 180 10.5 10 29.5 7 Apple Jacks Kelloggs cold 110 125 11 14 33.2 8 Basic 4 General … cold 130 210 18 8 37.0 9 Bran Chex Ralston … cold 90 200 15 6 49.1 10 Bran Flakes Post cold 90 210 13 5 53.3 #
